source.title: Biology Unit 3: Cell Membranes and Transport

concepts.name: Phospholipid bilayer
concepts.learningObjective: The student can describe the bilayer's structure and explain why it is a barrier to polar and charged substances.

concepts.name: Selective permeability
concepts.learningObjective: The student can predict whether a molecule crosses freely, needs a channel or carrier, or needs a pump.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain diffusion as the net result of random motion down a concentration gradient.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.learningObjective: The student can predict the direction of water movement from the solute concentrations on each side.

concepts.name: Tonicity: hypotonic, isotonic, hypertonic
concepts.learningObjective: The student can classify a solution as hypotonic, isotonic, or hypertonic relative to a cell and predict the cell's fate.

concepts.name: Facilitated diffusion
concepts.learningObjective: The student can distinguish facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion and from active transport.

concepts.name: Active transport
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain why moving a substance against its gradient requires ATP and give an example.

concepts.name: The sodium-potassium pump
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state what the sodium-potassium pump moves, in which directions, and why it matters.

concepts.name: Endocytosis and exocytosis
concepts.learningObjective: The student can order the steps of endocytosis and exocytosis and explain why both are active processes.

title: Inside a Cell

theme.setting: A tiny submarine crew on the outside of a living cell, heading for the nucleus

premise: Your crew shrank and is stuck on the outside of a cell. Open each gate as you walk inward to reach the nucleus.

characters.name: The Gatekeeper
characters.role: a very old pump protein who guards the last vault

encounters.targetMisconception: The membrane is a solid wall with holes in it.
encounters.prompt: Three chests describe the membrane, the thin skin around the cell. One is a mimic. Find its false claim.

statements.text: The membrane is a double layer of fat molecules called phospholipids
statements.explanation: Their heads like water, so they face out on both sides. Their oily tails point inward.

statements.text: The membrane is a stiff wall with fixed holes in it
statements.explanation: It flows like a film of oil. Its parts drift around, and things cross through it or through proteins.

statements.text: The middle of the membrane is oily and blocks most ions
statements.explanation: Ions are charged bits. They can't mix into the oily middle.

hints: Look at what each chest says the membrane is made of. Check whether it could bend and flow.
The membrane is fat molecules with oily tails. Oil can't hold a stiff shape, so it flows.
The chest about the oily middle blocking ions is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That chest tells the truth. Look for the claim that makes the membrane stiff.
encounters.debriefLine: The mimic said "The membrane is a stiff wall with fixed holes in it". Really, the membrane is a bilayer, a double layer of fat that flows like oil.

sourceRef.quote: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: the hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides and the hydrophobic tails point inward.

encounters.prompt: Sort the molecules waiting at the membrane. Can each one slip through the fat alone, or does it need a transport protein?

bins.label: Crosses the bilayer alone
bins.feature: small and nonpolar (no charged ends), so it mixes into the oily middle

bins.label: Needs a transport protein
bins.feature: polar or charged, so the oily middle pushes it away, or too big to squeeze through

items.why: Tiny, but it's charged. The oily middle pushes it away.
Big and polar. It rides a carrier protein.
It's made from fat, so it mixes straight through.
It's charged, so it needs a channel, a protein tunnel.

hints: Na+ and Cl- are tiny, smaller than some molecules on the list. Size alone won't tell you their group.
Check each one for a charge, like the + in Na+. The oily middle pushes charged things away.
The steroid hormone is the one people get wrong. Check if it's charged or made from fat.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Check for a charge before you check size. A tiny ion still gets blocked by the oily middle.
encounters.debriefLine: You sorted 6 molecules by whether they're charged or polar. The membrane picks what gets through, and that's called selective permeability.

sourceRef.quote: Ions and large polar molecules such as glucose cross only through transport proteins.

encounters.targetMisconception: Particles move toward empty space on purpose.
encounters.prompt: A cloud of dye is spreading through the tank. Three chests explain why. One of them is lying.

statements.text: Each dye particle moves at random, bumping into others
statements.explanation: Random jiggling is the only thing moving them.

statements.text: The dye particles head for the empty side on purpose
statements.explanation: No particle can steer. More end up on the empty side just by chance.

statements.text: Overall, the dye spreads from where it's crowded to where it isn't
statements.explanation: More particles start on the crowded side, so more cross from there.

hints: Pick one dye particle and follow it. Does it ever seem to know where the empty side is?
Each particle moves at random. More start on the crowded side, so more happen to cross from there.
The chest about particles bumping at random is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That chest tells the truth. Look for the claim that gives the dye a goal.
encounters.debriefLine: The mimic said "The dye particles head for the empty side on purpose". Diffusion is random moves spreading things out, with no plan at all.

sourceRef.quote: Because it is driven by the random motion of the particles themselves, diffusion requires no energy from the cell.

encounters.targetMisconception: Salt crosses the membrane instead of water.
encounters.prompt: A cell floats in very salty water. Three chests predict what happens. Point your lantern at the one that's lying.

statements.text: Water leaves the cell, moving toward the saltier side
statements.explanation: Water moves toward the side with more stuff dissolved in it.

statements.text: Salt rushes into the cell until both sides match
statements.explanation: Salt can't get through the fat layer. The water is what moves.

statements.text: The cell shrinks as it loses water
statements.explanation: Losing water makes the cell smaller.

hints: Two things could cross here, the water or the salt. Only one of them gets through the fat layer.
Water moves toward the side with more salt in it. Here that's the water outside the cell.
The chest about the cell shrinking is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That chest tells the truth. Look for the claim where the salt does the moving.
encounters.debriefLine: The mimic said "Salt rushes into the cell until both sides match". Osmosis means water crosses toward the saltier side, while the salt stays put.

sourceRef.quote: Water moves toward the side with the higher solute concentration, where the water concentration is lower.

encounters.targetMisconception: Hypertonic means the solution has more water.
encounters.prompt: Cells drift past in different liquids. Label each liquid by how much is dissolved in it compared to the cell.

waves.text: A red blood cell in pure water, swelling
waves.why: Less is dissolved outside than inside, so water flows in.
More is dissolved outside, so water flows out.

waves.text: A cell in a liquid that matches its own salt level, unchanged
waves.why: It's the same on both sides, so water doesn't move either way overall.

waves.text: A plant cell in salty soil water, wilting
waves.why: More salt outside pulls water out.

waves.text: A cell in a watery drink, about to burst
waves.why: Water rushes in from the watery drink.

hints: Each label is about the liquid around the cell. Compare how much is dissolved outside with inside.
Hyper means more dissolved outside, so water leaves. Hypo means less, so water comes in.
The cell in pure water is the one people mix up. Pure water has almost nothing dissolved in it.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Hypertonic means more stuff dissolved outside, and less water. So the cell loses water and shrinks.
encounters.debriefLine: You labeled each liquid by comparing it with the cell. That comparison is called tonicity.

sourceRef.quote: In a hypertonic solution the cell loses water and shrinks.

encounters.targetMisconception: If a protein is involved, the cell must be spending energy.
encounters.prompt: More cargo is waiting at the gates. Sort each one as passive (free) or active (costs ATP, the cell's energy).

bins.label: Passive, no ATP
bins.feature: moves from crowded to less crowded (down its gradient), with or without a protein

bins.label: Active, costs ATP
bins.feature: moves from less crowded to more crowded (against its gradient), so a pump spends energy

items.text: Glucose entering through a carrier protein, from high to low
items.why: A protein helps, but it's still downhill. No energy needed.
The channel just lets water through faster.

items.text: Na+ pumped out of a cell that already has little Na+
items.why: It's pushed toward the crowded side. That needs ATP.

items.text: K+ leaking out through an open channel, from high to low
items.why: It flows toward the less crowded side.

items.text: Protons (H+) pushed into a space that's already packed with them

hints: Look at the glucose. It uses a carrier protein, but check which way it's moving.
Ask if each one moves toward the crowded side or away from it. Only moving toward it costs ATP.
Water through the aquaporin often lands in the wrong group. Ask if anything has to push it.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Using a protein doesn't mean spending energy. Only moving toward the crowded side needs ATP.
encounters.debriefLine: You sorted 5 cases by which way they moved. A protein helping something downhill for free is called facilitated diffusion.

sourceRef.quote: Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins, but it is still passive: the molecules move down their gradient and the cell spends no energy.

encounters.targetMisconception: Transport always goes down the gradient.
encounters.prompt: The pump room hums. Three chests describe active transport, which means moving things with a pump. One is a mimic.

statements.text: Active transport moves things toward the more crowded side
statements.explanation: It pushes things from where there are few to where there are many.

statements.text: Active transport costs the cell ATP
statements.explanation: Pumps use energy to push uphill.

statements.text: Things only ever move toward the less crowded side, so pumps just speed them up
statements.explanation: Pumps push things uphill. That's why they need ATP.

hints: Look at the chest about ATP. Why would a cell spend energy just to move something?
Things drift toward the less crowded side for free. Paying ATP only makes sense for going the other way.
The chest about ATP is true. Compare the other two.
encounters.wrongFeedback: That chest tells the truth. Look for the claim that says things only go downhill.
encounters.debriefLine: The mimic said "Things only ever move toward the less crowded side, so pumps just speed them up". Active transport pumps things uphill, and the cell pays in ATP.

sourceRef.quote: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, from low concentration to high, and requires energy from ATP.

encounters.targetMisconception: The pump moves equal numbers of ions each way.
encounters.prompt: The sodium-potassium pump swaps sodium and potassium across the membrane. Rewire it by matching each part of one cycle to its value.

pairs.left: Cells that depend on it most
pairs.why: They use the difference in ions to send signals.

hints: Look at the counts for sodium and potassium. They aren't the same number.
Sodium goes out and potassium comes in. More ions leave than come in each cycle.
One of the 'out of the cell' cards is a trap. Only sodium leaves, and the counts aren't equal.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The pump is lopsided. More sodium goes out than potassium comes in, which leaves the inside a bit negative.
encounters.debriefLine: You matched 4 facts about the sodium-potassium pump. Each cycle sends 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, using 1 ATP.

sourceRef.quote: Each cycle of the sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in, at the cost of one ATP.

encounters.targetMisconception: Salt crosses the membrane instead of water.
encounters.prompt: Review time! Pick which way water moves for each cell before it drifts by.

waves.text: Cell with 2% salt inside, in a 10% salt bath
waves.why: More salt outside pulls water out.

waves.text: Cell with 2% salt inside, in distilled water
waves.why: Water flows toward the saltier cell.

waves.text: Cell with 0.9% salt inside, in 0.9% saline
waves.why: Same salt on both sides, so water moves both ways equally.

waves.text: Potato cells in a sugar syrup
waves.why: Syrup has far more sugar than the cells.

hints: Each card gives the salt inside the cell and in the bath around it. Compare those two.
Water moves toward the side with more salt or sugar. The salt itself stays put.
The potato cells are easy to get wrong. Syrup has far more sugar in it than a potato.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Water moves toward the side with more salt. The salt itself stays where it is.
encounters.debriefLine: Osmosis review. You worked out which way water moves in four cells, just from the salt levels.

sourceRef.quote: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

encounters.targetMisconception: Vesicle transport is passive because the cargo isn't pumped.
encounters.prompt: The big door only opens if the planks show how a large particle gets into the cell. One plank doesn't belong.

steps: The particle touches the outside of the membrane
The membrane folds inward around the particle
The pocket pinches off into a bubble called a vesicle
The vesicle carries the particle where it needs to go
decoys: The particle dissolves through the bilayer on its own

hints: Start with the particle outside the cell. Nothing can happen until it touches the membrane.
The membrane has to wrap around the particle before it can close the pocket.
Once the pocket pinches off, the particle is inside a bubble. What happens to that bubble last?
encounters.wrongFeedback: Check the order. The membrane can't pinch off a pocket before it wraps around the particle.
encounters.debriefLine: That's endocytosis, the cell swallowing something big. All 4 steps cost ATP, so it counts as active transport.

sourceRef.quote: In endocytosis the membrane folds inward around the cargo and pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell.

encounters.targetMisconception: Transport always goes down the gradient.
encounters.prompt: The Gatekeeper dumps mixed cargo at your feet. Sort each item by how it crosses the membrane.

bins.label: Simple diffusion
bins.feature: small and nonpolar, crosses the fat layer alone, downhill

bins.label: Facilitated diffusion
bins.feature: polar or charged, uses a channel or carrier, still downhill with no ATP

bins.label: Active transport
bins.feature: pushed uphill through a pump that spends ATP

items.text: O2 entering a cell that has used up its oxygen
items.why: Nonpolar and downhill, with no protein.

items.text: Glucose entering a muscle cell through a carrier, from high to low
items.why: A protein helps, but it's downhill.

items.text: Na+ pumped out against its gradient

items.why: Water uses a channel to cross.

items.text: CO2 leaving a cell that makes it
K+ pumped into a cell that already has lots of K+
Cl- entering through an open channel, from high to low
items.why: It's charged, so it needs a channel. It's still downhill.

hints: Look for 'pumped' and 'from high to low' in the cargo. Those words tell you which way each moves.
Anything pushed uphill is active. If it's downhill, ask if it can slip through the fat alone.
Water through the aquaporin is the tricky one. Check if it uses a protein.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Ask two things. Is it going uphill? If not, can it slip through the fat alone?
encounters.debriefLine: You sorted 7 cargo items by direction and charge. That covers simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport.

sourceRef.quote: If a cell runs out of ATP, its pumps stop and the gradients they maintain slowly dissipate.

intro.text: We've shrunk. That shiny film is the cell's skin. Open the gates and we can get to the nucleus.

outro.text: We made it to the nucleus. You opened every gate on the way in.

beats.text: Careful with the small ones. Being small doesn't mean they get in.
I have pumped for a billion years. Show me you know what costs energy.
Hrrm. All sorted right. You may pass.

pre.prompt: A cell sits in very salty water. Which way does water move?

choices: Pumping Na+ out against its gradient

pre.prompt: Which crosses the bilayer without any protein?

post.prompt: A freshwater fish cell sits in fresh water, which has far less salt than the cell. What happens?
A cell moves calcium from inside, where there's little, to outside, where there's lots. What kind of transport is this?
Na+ is tiny. Why can't it cross the bilayer on its own?
choices: It's charged, and the middle of the bilayer is oily
Sodium is toxic to the cell
